Transcript:
[00:00] Jenna Park: all right hi everyone thanks for joining today, um we'll kick off, this is Jenna from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Marcus and Anita on the SE side.
[00:08] Dr. Ravi Patel: hey thanks, Ravi here. we've got, uh, a packed agenda. this is about scoping the POC for our clinical assistant project. main need is snappy interactivity for docs and nurses.
[00:18] Maya Chen: hi Maya, infra on our side. want to make sure we size the workload and set realistic SLOs.
[00:24] Jenna Park: perfect, maybe to start, can you share the basic workload shape, like average prompt, average response, concurrency?
[00:31] Hannah Kim: fwiw our average prompt is around 50-80 tokens, responses about 80-140 tokens depending on the use case. concurrent active users during peak—roughly 60 simultaneous interactive sessions, but in a burst scenario we could see up to 200.
[00:45] Marcus Li: great that's helpful. so two parts we want to be explicit about: TTFT — time to first token — that's the client-perceived interactive latency, and TPOT — time to produce the whole response or time-to-last-token, which captures total request latency. they have different tradeoffs.
[01:05] Dr. Ravi Patel: quick clarifying question: is TTFT basically the thing that makes it feel responsive, like typing latency?
[01:09] Marcus Li: yep exactly. TTFT is the first byte, so if you're streaming it's how fast the first token arrives. TPOT or TtLT is the total time to get the complete answer, important for throughput and batch sizing. sometimes folks call it time-to-last-token or full-response latency.
[01:22] Luis Ortega: from security perspective we also care about any additional buffering from network or proxy, so measuring from client to first token and server-side to first token are both useful.
[01:31] Jenna Park: good point. for SLOs, let's propose a baseline and then we can adjust — given your workload profile, a common POC target is TTFT p95 < 250ms, p99 < 400ms; TPOT for a full ~120-token response p95 < 1.2s, p99 < 2.2s. are those in the right ballpark?
[01:50] Dr. Ravi Patel: that seems reasonable, though p99 matters a lot for us — clinical flows can't be sporadically slow. would love to tighten p99 if possible, maybe p99 ~ 1.2s for TPOT if we commit to dedicated infra?
[02:03] Marcus Li: that's realistic on dedicated GPUs with optimized kernels and prefix caching. hosted can hit similar p95s but p99 variability depends on multi-tenant noise and cold-starts. we should plan dedicated test runs if p99 is a firm requirement.
[02:18] Maya Chen: what about warm vs cold cache? our traffic has a lot of repeated prompts across clinicians so caching helps, but we need to understand cold-start behavior for new prompts or different models.
[02:29] Anita Gomez: we'll include both in the plan — warm-cache representative replay and cold-start tests with model spin-up times. for cold-start we measure from model allocation to first token; that's usually tens of seconds for a cold node if you need to pull weights, but we can use reserved capacity to avoid that.
[02:43] Hannah Kim: timeline wise we want a 4-week POC: week 1 collect sample prompts and traffic, week 2 run baseline hosted tests, week 3 run dedicated tests + tuning, week 4 validation and handoff. is that feasible?
[02:56] Marcus Li: yeah that aligns. we'll need access to your prompt set and traffic histograms. also permissions for replay — we usually obfuscate PHI and run on synthetic de-identified test data.
[03:07] Luis Ortega: yes we will provide de-identified prompts. plus we need to make sure encryption and audit logs are captured. we want to see KMS integration and proof of key controls.
[03:17] Jenna Park: action: we'll send the security pack and SOC2 summary, and a short doc on KMS + VPC options.
[03:23] Dr. Ravi Patel: great. switching back to measurement: what metrics will you capture during benchmarks?
[03:28] Marcus Li: we'll capture client-side TTFT/TTLT, server-side token emission times, p50/p95/p99, 95/99 CPU and GPU util, queue lengths, batch sizes, and KV-cache hit rates. also we record cold-start durations, and tail jitter. we'll produce a spreadsheet of results and dashboard snapshots.
[03:46] Maya Chen: do you provide the harness to replay traffic?
[03:49] Anita Gomez: yes, Marcus will share our load-generator scripts, and we have a harness that can replay at original inter-arrival times or accelerated. we'll include instructions to prime caches (e.g., run warm-up replay).
[03:59] Hannah Kim: curious about the benchmark surface—will you compare different quantization/precision settings?
[04:03] Marcus Li: we can. part of Redwood Optimize is recommending quantization levels per workload. for the POC we'll test FP16, 8-bit quantized variants if available, and measure quality regressions alongside latency. we'll keep an eval prompt set for quality checks — we won't just optimize latency at cost of clinically-relevant output.
[04:20] Dr. Ravi Patel: quality checks are a must. we need to ensure no hallucination regressions. can you tie regressions to prompt subsets?
[04:25] Marcus Li: absolutely, we'll run the evals per prompt group and flag any delta in key metrics.
[04:29] Luis Ortega: one more security note: if we run dedicated on-prem or VPC, we require customer-managed KMS or HSM. can Redwood support that?
[04:36] Jenna Park: yes, customer-managed KMS and HSM integration is supported for Private deployments; we'll include options in the security pack.
[04:42] Maya Chen: for the SLO targets you proposed earlier, how do we account for network tail or multi-region routing? our users are in US-East primarily.
[04:50] Marcus Li: we recommend measuring both client-to-inference and intra-datacenter times. for the POC we'll run tests from a probe in US-East to avoid cross-region noise; if you later expand, we can add regional tests and set routing policies.
[05:02] Hannah Kim: can we also capture cost per 1k requests for each configuration? budgeting matters.
[05:06] Marcus Li: yes we'll produce per-token and per-request cost estimates for hosted vs dedicated + reserved. Redwood Optimize will suggest batching and quantization knobs to reduce unit cost while respecting SLOs.
[05:15] Dr. Ravi Patel: ok to recap, I want the POC to prove: 1) TTFT p95 < 250ms and p99 < 400ms under representative concurrency, 2) TPOT (120-token) p95 < 1.2s and p99 < 2.2s for hosted, and tighter p99 if we move to dedicated, 3) quantization shouldn't degrade clinical quality beyond agreed thresholds, and 4) full measurement plan including warm/cold tests and security validation.
[05:40] Jenna Park: that's a great recap. we'll codify the SLOs in the runbook. one nuance: if your traffic has heavy long-context prompts, we may need to adjust TTFT expectations, since KV cache warm-up and attention compute increase tail latency.
[05:52] Maya Chen: noted, we'll include a few long-context cases in the sample set.
[05:56] Anita Gomez: for measurement specifics—proposed test matrix: concurrency levels [10, 60, 120, 200], prompt sizes [short (20-50), medium (50-100), long (100-400)], cache state [cold, warm], model variants [fp16, 8-bit]. we run 3 iterations per cell, capture p50/p95/p99, GPU util, batch sizes, and report.
[06:16] Marcus Li: also we'll capture histogram of per-token emission times to see where tail is coming from — e.g., kernel stalls, queuing, or IO.
[06:23] Luis Ortega: what about instrumentation? we need tracing IDs to correlate client logs with Redwood logs for audit.
[06:28] Jenna Park: we can include trace correlation IDs in the harness; Redwood Console will surface traces and per-request metadata including route, model version, and user token (obfuscated).
[06:37] Dr. Ravi Patel: what happens if we don't meet p99 targets in hosted during POC? do you have fallback strategies?
[06:43] Marcus Li: yes, we can propose automated fallback to a lower-latency model variant or route to dedicated pool. Redwood supports routing policies and automatic fallbacks; we'll include that as an operational option.
[06:53] Hannah Kim: final question on timeline: can you run hosted baseline next week and dedicated the following week?
[06:58] Jenna Park: we can start hosted baseline as soon as we get the prompt set and replay permissions — so if you provide those by 2026-04-26 we can run baseline the week of 2026-04-29 and dedicated the week of 2026-05-04.
[07:11] Maya Chen: yes we will target 4/26 for artifacts.
[07:14] Jenna Park: great. any other blockers?
[07:16] Luis Ortega: confirm we'll get the security pack and KMS options doc.
[07:19] Jenna Park: yes, sending by 4/24.
[07:22] Dr. Ravi Patel: thanks all. let's reconvene after the hosted baseline results.
[07:25] Jenna Park: thanks everyone, we'll send calendar invite for the perf test and post a runbook link.

Recap / Agreed SLOs (as stated in call):
- TTFT (time to first token): target p95 < 250ms, p99 < 400ms (interactive usage)
- TPOT / full-response (approx 120 tokens): target hosted p95 < 1.2s, p99 < 2.2s; dedicated can aim to reduce p99 nearer to ~1.2s if needed

Measurement Plan (high level):
1) Data collection: Lumen provides de-identified sample prompt set and 14-day traffic histogram (by 2026-04-26).
2) Warm-cache tests: replay representative traffic with cache primed, measure TTFT/TPOT across concurrency matrix.
3) Cold-start tests: measure model spin-up times and cold TTFT for new requests.
4) Model/config matrix: test fp16, 8-bit quantized, and recommended kernel/config tuning.
5) Metrics: p50/p95/p99 TTFT and TPOT, per-token emission histogram, GPU util, queue lengths, batch sizes, cache hit-rate, cost per 1k requests.
6) Quality checks: run eval prompt subset for hallucination/regression detection after each config change.
7) Reporting: Redwood to deliver a spreadsheet and dashboard screens, plus recommended config for production.
